But that would make persistence through time impossible for ordinary objects as well as persons. Something can remain numerically one thing while changing qualitatively. The same sandwich can be cool at 11:00 and warm at 1:00; strict sameness does not require sameness of every property across time.

So the fact that the child had different height, vocabulary, goals, and memories does not show that the child was only similar to Maya. Those are qualitative differences. The real question is whether the child-stage and the current adult-stage are installments in one causal sequence. On the lecture’s account of diachronic identity, persistence over time consists in belonging to a continuous, causally connected history.

That is the form a personal identity claim must take as well. Saying "I am the child in the photo" is not using some special kind of personal sameness unrelated to object identity. It is a standard identity claim applied to a person: one being present in temporally distinct installments.

So Maya’s reasoning fails because change does not defeat identity. What would need to be true is not perfect qualitative sameness, but a single continuing causal history linking the child and the adult as one person over time.
problems.explanation: Tests the distinction between numerical and qualitative identity, and the diachronic model of persistence as a causal sequence. A strong answer must show why change in properties does not by itself refute identity over time.
problems.hint: Separate 'having the same properties' from 'being the same thing.'

problems.prompt: In discussing a house fire, Omar says: "The cause was the toaster. That's obvious. The toaster caused the fire." Priya replies: "No object can literally be a cause. Only something like the toaster's overheating at 2:10 a.m., together with nearby paper towels and an active electrical current, could explain the fire. And even that wouldn't be the whole story." Who is closer to the view in the lecture, and why? In your answer, say what needs to be corrected in Omar's statement and why Priya also says the relevant cause would not be the whole story.
problems.correctAnswer:
Priya is much closer to the lecture’s view. The first correction is logical: causes are events, not objects. So the toaster itself is not literally the cause any more than a rock itself is the cause of a broken window. What does causal work is some event involving the object, such as the toaster’s overheating, sparking, or igniting nearby material at a particular time.

Priya is also right to include surrounding factors, because what we ordinarily single out as "the cause" is rarely a condition that is sufficient by itself. The overheating alone might not have produced a fire if there had been no combustible material nearby, or if the power had cut out, or if a safety device had worked. That means the cited factor is only part of a larger sufficient condition.

This is exactly the kind of case for which the INUS analysis is useful. The overheating event would be an insufficient but non-redundant part of an unnecessary but sufficient condition for the fire. It is insufficient by itself; it matters as one essential element in a larger cluster. And that larger cluster is unnecessary in the sense that the house might have burned by some entirely different route.

So Omar’s sentence can be repaired, but only by replacing the object with an event and by recognizing that the event cited is ordinarily a partial cause rather than the whole causal story.
problems.explanation: Tests two causation principles: causes are events rather than objects, and ordinary causes are partial causes captured by Mackie's INUS analysis. A strong answer must correct object-talk into event-talk and explain why the selected cause is not by itself the whole explanation.
problems.hint: First ask: what happened involving the toaster? Then ask: would that event alone have guaranteed the fire?

title: Homework 4 — Ethics, Value, and Law
instructions: Untimed practice. Answer each question in a few complete sentences, in your own words.

problems.prompt: Mara says, "People keep confusing ethics with practical advice. Suppose a manager can increase profits by quietly dumping toxic waste into a river and is certain no one will trace it back to the company. In that case the dumping is good, because it helps the manager achieve his goal." Evaluate Mara’s reasoning. In your answer, explain whether the word "good" is being used in the right sense for an ethical conclusion, and show how the case should be assessed if we are doing ethics rather than strategy.
problems.correctAnswer:
Mara’s reasoning trades on an ambiguity in the word "good." In one sense, the dumping might be good instrumentally: if the manager’s sole aim is profit, and if he really will avoid detection, then the act may serve his practical interest. But that does not establish that the act is ethically good. The lecture’s point is that ethics is not the study of what advances an agent’s advantage; it is the analysis of normative categories such as good, bad, commendable, and condemnable in their intrinsic sense.

So if we are doing ethics rather than strategy, we must ask not whether the act benefits the manager, but what sort of act it is apart from that advantage. Quietly poisoning a river for profit harms others and treats their welfare as expendable. That makes it ethically condemnable even if it is clever or effective from the manager’s perspective. The fact that it helps him reach his goal is therefore irrelevant to its intrinsic moral status.

A proper reply to Mara is: you have shown, at most, that the act is useful to the agent. Ethics asks a different question—whether the act itself falls under a favorable normative category. In this case it does not. It is not commendable because it is profitable; it is condemnable despite being profitable.
problems.explanation: Tests the distinction between descriptive/strategic assessment and ethical assessment, especially instrumental versus intrinsic goodness. A strong answer must show why success for the agent does not by itself amount to ethical goodness.
problems.hint: Ask whether the conclusion would still seem "good" if you ignored the manager’s advantage and looked only at the act itself.

problems.prompt: During a discussion about corruption, Eli says, "Moral arguments are pointless. When Priya says, 'Bribing inspectors is wrong,' she is just expressing disgust. I happen not to feel disgust about it, so we are not really disagreeing about anything." Priya replies that Eli is mistaken. Using the lecture’s framework, explain who is closer to the truth and why. Your answer should use this case to show what would be missing if moral claims were only expressions of feeling.
problems.correctAnswer:
Priya is closer to the truth. Eli treats her statement as if it were merely a shout of disapproval—something like "boo bribery!" But the lecture argues that moral judgments are not exhausted by felt attitude. A person can make a sincere moral judgment coolly, without any vivid emotion at all. So even if Priya does feel disgust, the content of her claim is not identical with that feeling.

More importantly, her claim presents bribery as having a certain significance in the world: as corrupt, harmful, and obstructive of the conditions under which people like us flourish. That is why moral disagreement behaves like real disagreement. Priya and Eli are not just making different noises. She is saying something that can be correct or mistaken, and she is taking Eli to be wrong about the practice itself.

If moral utterances were only expressions of feeling, then there would be no contradiction between them. Priya would be cheering one way, Eli another. But that is not how the exchange works. They argue, demand reasons, and try to correct one another. That makes sense only if moral claims have a factual component. The relevant emotions are themselves belief-like or doxastic: they embody a view about what damages or benefits beings like us. So Eli’s reduction of morality to mere attitude leaves out the cognitive, truth-apt aspect of Priya’s judgment.
problems.explanation: Tests the critique of emotivism and the move to moral realism. A strong answer must explain why moral disagreement is not just clashing attitudes and why ethical judgments are answerable to facts about harm, benefit, and flourishing.
problems.hint: Focus on the difference between merely feeling disgust and judging that something is actually corrupt or harmful.

problems.prompt: Jon says, "Every action is really done for pleasure. Look at Lena: she spends her weekends teaching adult literacy classes for free, and she admits that helping her students makes her feel deeply satisfied. So the satisfaction must be the real reason she does it. Her talk about caring for education is just decoration." Assess Jon’s argument using the distinctions from the lecture. In particular, explain what further question we should ask before concluding that Lena acts for pleasure.
problems.correctAnswer:
Jon’s argument is too quick because it ignores the distinction between acting in order to bring about a result and acting while knowing that the result will occur. From the fact that Lena gets satisfaction from teaching, it does not follow that her aim is to obtain that satisfaction. She may instead teach because she sees value in helping people learn, and the satisfaction may arise because she values that activity.

That is exactly the pattern emphasized in the lecture. Pleasure often accompanies action when the action is already regarded as worth doing. The order of explanation matters. If Lena values literacy, opportunity, and the good of her students, then helping them can please her precisely because she sees it as valuable. In that case the pleasure is reflective accompaniment, not the object sought.

So the further question is counterfactual: if the valuable end could be achieved without the pleasurable feeling, or if the same pleasure could be produced by some activity she regarded as worthless, what would she choose? If she would still teach because she cares about the students’ good, then Jon’s hedonistic interpretation fails. His inference would work only if the pleasure were what she was after in the way a drug user seeks a sensation. But the mere presence of satisfaction does not establish that. It may instead depend on a prior recognition of value.
problems.explanation: Tests the rejection of psychological hedonism/egoism by using the intended-versus-foreseen distinction and the claim that pleasure often follows perceived value. A strong answer must show why enjoyment does not prove that pleasure is the motive.
problems.hint: Ask whether Lena would still do it if she thought the work was worthwhile but it stopped being enjoyable.

problems.prompt: A city has a law requiring all building contractors to file detailed safety reports before construction begins. Devin skips the report because his project is tiny, he has already checked everything carefully, and in this particular case no one is endangered. He says, "Since no harm came from my exception, I did nothing morally wrong. The law is just bureaucracy." Using the lecture’s account of legality, morality, and legal obligation, evaluate Devin’s defense.
problems.correctAnswer:
Devin is right that legality and morality are not identical: violating a law does not automatically make an act immoral, and the harmlessness of one instance is morally relevant. But his defense is still inadequate, because it treats the case only at the local level and ignores what legal obligation is for.

On the lecture’s view, a legal obligation is not a mysterious nonmoral force. It is a kind of moral obligation to comply with a public system of rules that people depend on for the protection of rights and important social goods. Safety-report requirements are not justified solely by what happens in each isolated case. They belong to a framework meant to make oversight reliable, prevent corner-cutting, and maintain accountability before disasters occur.

So even if Devin’s single project caused no actual harm, that does not settle whether his disobedience was morally permissible. The question is whether making ad hoc exceptions for oneself is compatible with sustaining the sort of dependable rule-governed system that protects people in general. In many cases it is not. His argument—"no harm here, therefore no moral wrong"—misses the systemic rationale of law.

A better assessment is: the act may be morally wrong because it breaches a morally justified legal framework, even though the immediate outcome in this one case happened to be harmless. The obligation is to uphold the system, not merely to avoid visible harm each time.
problems.explanation: Tests the relation between legality and morality and the rule-utilitarian structure of legal obligation. A strong answer must show why one-case harmlessness does not by itself defeat a duty to comply with a rights-protecting system.
problems.hint: Distinguish the effect of this one act from the justification for having the rule at all.

problems.prompt: Nora argues as follows: "The sentence 'Unicorns do not exist' must still be about something, because grammatically it has a subject term, 'unicorns.' So there must be some strange object—perhaps a non-real unicorn—that the sentence is referring to. Otherwise the sentence could not be meaningful or true." Using the methodological lesson from the lecture, explain what has gone wrong in Nora’s reasoning and how an analytic philosopher should respond.
problems.correctAnswer:
What has gone wrong is that Nora is trusting surface grammar as a guide to logical form. Because the sentence contains what looks like a subject term, she assumes there must be a thing for the sentence to be about. But the lecture warns that this move generates pseudo-entities by reading ontology off grammar.

An analytic response begins by asking what must actually be the case for the sentence to make sense and be true. "Unicorns do not exist" need not be analyzed as attributing a property to some peculiar object called a non-real unicorn. Rather, it says that nothing satisfies the relevant condition—roughly, that there is no thing that is a unicorn. Once the statement is understood in that way, its truth requires no commitment to a strange item that both is and is not there.

Nora’s proposal is self-undermining in the same style as the lecture’s warning about impossible objects. If there really were an object answering to the term in the way she suggests, then the original claim of nonexistence would be compromised. So the temptation is created by sentence form, not by logical necessity.

The methodological lesson is general: when an apparently ordinary sentence seems to force absurd metaphysics, we should reconsider its logical structure instead of inventing bizarre furniture of the world. Philosophy corrects surface illusion by analysis; it does not preserve the illusion by multiplying entities.
problems.explanation: Tests the capstone method of correcting surface grammatical form by analyzing logical form. A strong answer must show why grammatical subject position does not automatically imply a corresponding object in reality.
problems.hint: Try paraphrasing the sentence without treating 'unicorns' as naming a mysterious object.

title: Unit 4 Test — Ethics, Value, and Law
instructions: Timed test. Answer each question thoroughly and in your own words.

problems.prompt: Mira tells her classmate: "Cheating on the exam was good because it raised my scholarship chances and probably won't hurt me." Her classmate replies: "Then ethics just tells people how to get what they want efficiently." Using this exchange, assess both claims. Explain what each speaker is getting right or wrong, and say how the case should be described if we are being careful about the kind of 'good' ethics studies.
problems.correctAnswer:
Mira is using "good" in an instrumental sense: the cheating helped serve her practical interest by improving her chances at money and success. In that limited strategic sense, her act may indeed be advantageous to her. But the lecture insists that ethics is not about what is useful to the agent as agent. It is about intrinsic goodness and other normative categories such as commendable, condemnable, just, and unjust. So Mira’s statement trades on an ambiguity in "good." She moves from "good for me" to the suggestion that the act is ethically good, and that move fails.

Her classmate is also wrong if he concludes that ethics is simply a manual for efficient desire-satisfaction. That would collapse ethics into strategy. Ethics instead asks what conditions an act must satisfy to count as praiseworthy or condemnable apart from its usefulness to the person doing it. On that standard, cheating is not vindicated by benefiting Mira.

So the careful description is: cheating may be instrumentally good for Mira if it advances her interests, but that says nothing by itself in favor of its ethical status. The ethical question is whether the act is intrinsically good or bad, commendable or condemnable. And once we ask that question, the appeal to scholarship advantage is beside the point.
problems.explanation: Tests the distinction between descriptive/normative categories and, especially, instrumental versus intrinsic goodness. A strong answer must show why 'good for me' does not settle whether an act is ethically good.
problems.hint: Ask whether the benefit cited is a benefit to the agent, or a reason the act belongs under a normative category like commendable.

problems.prompt: During a jury discussion, Lena says, "Calling the fraudster 'dishonest' just means I dislike him. Moral language is basically booing and cheering." Another juror answers, "No, because even if you felt oddly fond of him, he could still be dishonest." Evaluate this disagreement. In your answer, use the case to explain whether Lena's view can make sense of moral disagreement and correction in the jury room.
problems.correctAnswer:
The second juror is right. Lena’s view treats moral judgment as mere expression of feeling, but that cannot explain what is happening in the jury room. The jurors are not simply venting opposed attitudes, like one person cheering and another booing. They are trying to determine whether the fraudster really acted dishonestly. That practice of arguing, correcting, and accusing one another of getting it wrong makes sense only if moral claims have a factual component.

The case also shows why present feeling cannot be identical with moral judgment. A juror might personally like the defendant—perhaps he reminds her of a relative—while still judging that he is dishonest. Or she might feel disgust toward him for irrelevant reasons yet still have to ask whether the evidence actually supports the moral description. That is exactly the sort of separation between immediate sentiment and judgment emphasized in the lecture.

So Lena is wrong twice. First, moral utterances are not reducible to emotional noises. Second, even when emotion is involved, it is not brute noise but embodies a view about value—here, a view that the defendant’s conduct is deceptive and damaging in ways relevant to human flourishing and social trust. Because that content can fit or misfit the facts, the judgment is assessable as correct or incorrect.
problems.explanation: Tests the rejection of emotivism and the move to moral realism. A strong answer must explain why moral disagreement in the case is more than conflicting feelings and why ethical judgment can outstrip current emotion.
problems.hint: Focus on what the jurors are doing when they dispute, revise, and demand evidence.

problems.prompt: Owen says, "Every action is selfish. Take Priya: she spends every Saturday tutoring struggling students, and she admits it makes her happy. So she really does it for the pleasure." A friend replies, "That doesn't follow. She may value the students' improvement, and the happiness may come from that." Using this case, decide whose reasoning is better. Be explicit about the difference between acting for a result and acting while knowing or experiencing that result.
problems.correctAnswer:
The friend’s reasoning is better. Owen assumes that because Priya gets pleasure from tutoring, pleasure must be the thing she is aiming at. But the lecture rejects that inference. We must distinguish acting in order to bring about some result from acting while knowing that the result will occur, or while enjoying the activity because one values it. Priya’s happiness may be a consequence of her tutoring without being her purpose.

The best explanation of the case is that Priya sees value in helping the students learn. Because she regards that activity as worthwhile, doing it gives her pleasure. The order of explanation matters: value first, pleasure second. If she thought tutoring these students was pointless, the same activity likely would not please her. So the mere presence of happiness does not show selfish motivation.

Owen’s argument repeats the mistake criticized in psychological hedonism and egoism. It treats all enjoyed action as if it were like taking a drug for a rush. But the lecture insists on a contrast between pursuing pleasure as such and taking pleasure in what one sees as worth doing. Priya’s case fits the latter pattern. To show selfishness, Owen would need evidence that she helps solely for the pleasant feeling and would be equally happy harming the students if that produced the same sensation. Nothing in the case supports that.
problems.explanation: Tests the critique of psychological hedonism/egoism via the distinction between intended ends and foreseen or accompanying pleasure. A strong answer must apply that distinction to Priya rather than merely state the doctrine.
problems.hint: Would Priya still tutor if the activity mattered to the students but was less enjoyable? That question helps reveal her aim.

problems.prompt: In a discussion group, Daniel argues: "Religion is irrational because any belief worth keeping must be dropped the moment contrary evidence appears. So a genuinely religious believer should revise belief exactly as a scientist does." Another student answers: "Then you are no longer criticizing religion as religion; you're demanding that it stop being what it is." Analyze this exchange. Does Daniel's attack, as framed, hit its target?
problems.correctAnswer:
On the lecture’s view, Daniel’s attack misses its target. His criticism assumes from the outset that all respectable belief must be proportioned to evidence and abandoned when the evidence turns against it. But that is precisely the scientific attitude the chapter contrasts with religious commitment. If religious belief is, as the lecture claims, not governed by ordinary evidential dependence, then faulting it for failing to behave like science simply presupposes the very standard religion rejects.

That does not show religion is true or immune from all criticism. The point is narrower and conceptual. Daniel says he is criticizing religion, but his argument really says: "Religion would be acceptable only if it were evidence-responsive in the same way as science." Once framed that way, the student’s reply is apt: Daniel is not attacking religion on its own terms; he is demanding a change of category.

The case mirrors the lecture’s example of someone who adjusts belief day by day according to available data. Such a person may come to believe in God, but to that extent he exhibits a scientific posture, not distinctively religious faith. So Daniel’s objection begs the question. It assumes that contrary evidence ought to function as defeater in exactly the way a religious believer, qua religious believer, need not accept.
problems.explanation: Tests the claim that rationalistic attacks on religion often beg the question by imposing a scientific norm of evidence on a category not defined by that norm. A strong answer must explain why the criticism is category-mistaken rather than merely harsh.
problems.hint: Ask what standard Daniel assumes all belief must satisfy, and whether the lecture treats that standard as internal to religion.

problems.prompt: A city bans unlicensed street medicine. During a transit strike, a trained nurse whose license renewal is delayed treats an unconscious stranger on the sidewalk and saves his life. A police officer says, "What she did was wrong because it was illegal." Another bystander says, "No, illegality proves nothing; law and morality are totally unrelated." Evaluate both responses. Then explain whether the nurse may still have some moral reason to respect the licensing system even if this illegal act was morally justified.
problems.correctAnswer:
Both responses are too crude. The officer is wrong because legality is not sufficient for morality. An act can be illegal yet morally justified, just as the lecture insists that legal status and moral status can come apart. In this case, saving the stranger’s life plausibly makes the nurse’s action morally right despite violating the licensing rule.

But the bystander goes too far in the opposite direction. From the fact that legality and morality can diverge, it does not follow that they are unrelated. The lecture argues that legal obligation is itself a kind of moral obligation: the obligation to comply with a system on which people depend for the protection of rights and important social goods. Licensing rules for medical practice fit that structure well, since they help secure competence, accountability, and public safety.

So the nurse may have acted morally in this emergency while the law still has moral significance. She can acknowledge a standing moral reason to support and normally comply with the licensing system because of its systemic value, even though this particular instance justified an exception. That is exactly why we should not assess the rule only at the level of immediate local outcome. The rule belongs to a broader protective framework. Thus illegal need not mean immoral, but the law is not morally irrelevant either.
problems.explanation: Tests the lecture’s middle position between identifying law with morality and severing them completely, plus the systemic justification of legal rules. A strong answer must show both why the act may be morally right and why the legal rule still has moral force.
problems.hint: Separate the moral assessment of this emergency action from the moral point of having a public legal system at all.

title: Final Examination — Comprehensive
instructions: Timed comprehensive final covering all four units. Answer each question thoroughly in your own words.

problems.prompt: During a hike, Mira sees dark clouds and says, "Those clouds mean rain." A few minutes later, she texts her brother, "I'm fine," but she is actually trying to reassure him so he will stop worrying; she does not literally mean that she is fine, since she is exhausted and scared. Her brother later tells a friend, "When Mira wrote 'I'm fine,' the sentence meant that she was not in danger, so that's what she meant by it too." Evaluate the brother's reasoning. In your answer, sort out the different roles played by "mean" in this case and explain exactly where his inference goes wrong.
problems.correctAnswer:
The brother runs together distinct senses of “mean.” When Mira says the clouds “mean rain,” that is evidential meaning: the clouds are evidence of rain. Nothing linguistic is involved. When she texts “I’m fine,” the sentence has a linguistic meaning: it says that she is fine. But what she means by sending it, in the psychological sense, may be different. Here the case stipulates that she intends to calm her brother, not to state literally that she is fine. So her psychological meaning is something like: stop worrying, I can manage, or do not panic.

The brother’s mistake is to infer from the sentence’s linguistic meaning to the speaker’s psychological meaning. That inference is invalid because a speaker can use words with one literal content to convey something else. Irony, understatement, evasion, and reassurance all show this. The sentence does indeed mean, linguistically, that Mira is fine; but it does not follow that this is what she meant by uttering it. Nor does the evidential use of “mean” with the clouds support anything about language. The case contains three different relations, and his argument fails because it treats them as one.
problems.explanation: Tests the lecture’s claim that “meaning” is deeply equivocal: evidential meaning, psychological meaning, and linguistic meaning are distinct. A strong answer must apply those distinctions to diagnose an equivocation in the brother’s reasoning.
problems.hint: Ask separately: What is evidence for what? What does the sentence literally say? What was the speaker trying to get across?

problems.prompt: Leo glances across a parking lot and immediately says, "That's my sister's bicycle—the one stolen last month." All he can actually see from where he stands is a blue bicycle with a dented front basket and a torn seat cover. A friend replies, "If you can see that bicycle, then your eyes are telling you it is that very bicycle." Using the course's account of perception, explain whether the friend is right. Distinguish what perception gives Leo from what Leo may be adding from memory and background knowledge.
problems.correctAnswer:
The friend is not right. On the view from the lecture, perception is purely descriptive: it gives Leo the truth of an existence-claim, not the identity of a particular object as such. What his eyes tell him is something like: there exists, here and now, a bicycle of such-and-such appearance—blue, dented basket, torn seat cover, in this location. If some object uniquely satisfies that descriptive content, then that object is what he perceives.

But his eyes do not tell him that it is his sister’s very bicycle, as opposed to a perfect duplicate. The visual information is consistent with there being another bike that matches the visible description, and even consistent with the stolen bike no longer existing. So the claim of identity outruns perception itself.

Leo may still be reasonable in believing it is the stolen bicycle, but that would depend on background knowledge, memory, and inference: perhaps he knows the combination of features is highly distinctive, and he knows the bike was often left in this area. The immediate recognition may be psychologically instantaneous, yet philosophically it includes more than perception alone. Perception supplies the descriptive content; conception and prior knowledge supply the identification.
problems.explanation: Tests the thesis that perception gives descriptive existence-claims rather than bare particulars or identity facts. A strong answer must separate perceptual content from what is inferred or “read into” experience.
problems.hint: Focus on whether the visual message rules out a perfect duplicate.

problems.prompt: At dinner, Priya says, "Arun might never have become a doctor." Ben answers, "No, that's impossible. 'Arun' means 'the doctor in our family,' so if he weren't a doctor, it wouldn't be Arun you were talking about." Critically assess Ben's reply using the course's treatment of names and descriptions. Explain how Priya's claim can make sense even if Arun is in fact the only doctor in the family.
problems.correctAnswer:
Ben’s reply mistakes a proper name for a description. On the course view, a genuine proper name denotes without connoting: “Arun” contributes its bearer, not a descriptive condition such as “the doctor in our family.” A definite description works by picking out whoever uniquely satisfies some condition; a name does not work that way.

So Priya’s modal claim makes perfect sense. She is talking about that very individual, Arun, and saying that in another possible situation he might have failed medical school, chosen another career, or never applied. The name still refers to Arun across those possibilities, because it rigidly designates the same person wherever that person exists. By contrast, “the doctor in our family” is non-rigid: in another possible world, it might refer to someone else, or to no one at all.

Ben’s argument would only work if understanding the name required building the description into its literal meaning. But that is exactly what the lecture rejects. The fact that Arun happens to be the only doctor in the family in the actual world does not make being that doctor part of what the name means. Priya therefore can coherently say that Arun might never have become a doctor.
problems.explanation: Tests Mill’s thesis that names denote without connoting and the linked idea that names are rigid designators while descriptions are not. A strong answer must show why substituting a description for a name distorts modal reasoning.
problems.hint: Ask whether a different career for Arun would make the name stop referring to him.

problems.prompt: Nadia argues: "Every object in this box is a cube. This paperweight is in the box. So this paperweight has six faces." Omar argues: "This cafeteria's soup has tasted fresh every day for three months. So today's soup will be fresh too." A classmate says both arguments are equally strong because each starts from premises and reaches a conclusion. Compare the two inferences using the course's distinction between deduction and induction. Explain what would have to be true for each conclusion to be secure.
problems.correctAnswer:
The classmate is right that both are inferences, since each forms a new belief from prior beliefs. But they are not equally strong in the same way, because they aim at different standards. Nadia’s inference is deductive. If every object in the box is a cube and the paperweight is in the box, then it cannot be false that the paperweight has six faces, assuming the reasoning is non-faulty and “cube” is understood correctly. The premises, if true, rule out the conclusion’s falsity.

Omar’s inference is inductive. Even if it is true that the soup has been fresh every day for three months, today’s soup could still be spoiled. The premises give some reason for the conclusion, but they do not guarantee it. The conclusion remains defeasible.

So what is required differs. For Nadia’s conclusion to be secure, we need true premises plus valid deductive form. For Omar’s conclusion to count as strong, we need the past pattern to provide good support, but even then the conclusion is not made certain. The mistake is treating “has premises and a conclusion” as enough to erase the distinction between reasoning that excludes error and reasoning that only makes error less likely.
problems.explanation: Tests the distinction between deductive and inductive inference. A strong answer must apply the criterion of impossibility of true premises with false conclusion to one case, and deny it in the other.
problems.hint: Could the premises be true while the conclusion is false?

problems.prompt: Jalen believes that the museum closes at 5 p.m. His evidence is this: (1) he saw a sign yesterday that looked like it said "Open until 5," and (2) this morning a reliable friend told him, "The museum still closes at 5." Another friend says testimony is a fourth basic source of justification alongside perception, introspection, and inference. Using the course material, explain how Jalen may or may not be justified, and whether testimony should count as an ultimate source here.
problems.correctAnswer:
On the course view, testimony is not a fourth ultimate source of justification. The ultimate sources are perceptual evidence, introspective evidence, and rational inference. Testimony can still justify, but only derivatively. In Jalen’s case, the sign contributes perceptual evidence if he really saw it clearly enough. His friend’s statement can also support the belief, but only because Jalen has reasons—grounded in perception and past inference—to regard that friend as reliable, sincere, and competent about the museum’s hours.

So Jalen may well be justified, but the structure of the justification matters. If his visual experience of the sign was weak or ambiguous, the perceptual support is thin. The testimonial support then depends on an inference from background evidence, such as: this friend usually reports such matters accurately; nothing suggests a change in hours; therefore the report is probably correct. That makes testimony a channel by which beliefs are acquired, not an irreducible source of warrant.

The other friend’s mistake is classificatory but philosophically important. If every socially acquired belief counted as basic in its own right, we would lose sight of what actually underwrites its credibility. Testimony can transmit justification, but it does not replace the more fundamental sources from which that justification must ultimately derive.
problems.explanation: Tests the lecture’s restriction of ultimate sources of justification to perception, introspection, and rational inference, while allowing testimony as derivative. A strong answer must explain both how testimony can help and why it is not basic.
problems.hint: Ask what makes the speaker worth trusting in the first place.

problems.prompt: In a seminar, Rowan says, "I'm skeptical that memory is reliable." Another student replies, "Then you must believe all your memories are false." Evaluate that reply. Then consider a second claim Rowan makes: "Because memory can mislead us, no belief based on memory is ever justified." Using the course's account of skepticism, explain the difference between Rowan's first and second positions and whether the second really follows from the first.
problems.correctAnswer:
The reply to Rowan’s first remark is mistaken. On the course’s account, skepticism is doubt, not disbelief. To be skeptical that memory is reliable is not to believe that every memory is false. It is to suspend acceptance, or at least to question whether memory supplies adequate reason for beliefs of that kind. So the first position concerns insufficiency of warrant, not the truth of the opposite claim.

Rowan’s second statement is much stronger. It no longer merely withholds confidence in memory’s reliability; it asserts a universal negative thesis about justification: that no memory-based belief is ever justified. That does not automatically follow from skepticism in the first sense. One might doubt whether memory is generally reliable without claiming to have established that it never justifies anything.

Indeed, the second claim seems closer to a dogmatic anti-memory position than to skepticism as characterized in the lecture. The skeptic’s characteristic move is category-level doubt about whether we have enough reason to accept a class of claims. That is different from positively concluding that all such claims lack justification. So the second claim requires argument beyond the first. Doubt about a source does not by itself yield the sweeping conclusion that every use of that source is epistemically worthless.
problems.explanation: Tests the lecture’s insistence that skepticism is suspension of acceptance about a class of claims, not belief in their negation. A strong answer must distinguish doubt from disbelief and resist an unwarranted slide from one to the other.
problems.hint: Compare 'I am not convinced' with 'I am convinced the opposite is true.'

problems.prompt: After a storm, a large branch is found on a crushed car. Tessa says, "That branch caused the damage." Malik answers, "No object can be a cause. Only an event can be a cause. So your statement is completely false." Using the course's account of causation, assess both remarks. Rewrite Tessa's claim in a way that preserves what is right about ordinary speech while respecting the philosophical analysis.
problems.correctAnswer:
Malik is right about the underlying analysis but wrong to treat ordinary speech as simply false. The course’s view is that causes are events, not objects. So strictly speaking, the branch itself is not the cause. What caused the damage was an event involving the branch—its falling onto the car, or its striking the roof with a certain mass, speed, and trajectory during the storm. Causal explanation relates one occurrence to another occurrence.

Still, Tessa’s statement is not worthless. It is ordinary elliptical speech. When people say “the branch caused the damage,” they usually mean that some event involving the branch did. Philosophy’s role here is to make explicit the structure concealed by everyday shorthand, not to pretend that everyday speakers never manage to communicate.

A better formulation would be: “The branch’s falling onto the car caused the damage,” or more precisely, “The event of the branch striking the car roof during the storm caused the roof to collapse.” That preserves the truth in Tessa’s remark while putting the cause in the correct category.

The case also helps distinguish an object from its causal properties. The branch is not itself the cause, but properties such as its weight and momentum can be causally relevant features of the event.
problems.explanation: Tests the claim that causes belong to the category of events rather than objects, while ordinary object-cause talk is elliptical. A strong answer must correct the category mistake without overcorrecting into linguistic pedantry.
problems.hint: Turn the noun phrase naming a thing into a phrase naming something that happened.

problems.prompt: A city passes a law forbidding volunteers from distributing food in public parks without a permit. Ava ignores the rule and hands out meals to unhoused people after a blizzard. When fined, she says, "What I did was legal in the only sense that matters, because it was morally right." A city official replies, "If it was illegal, it was immoral; otherwise law would have no authority." Using the course material, evaluate both claims and explain what relation between law and morality the lecture supports.
problems.correctAnswer:
Both claims are too crude. Ava is wrong to collapse legality into morality. On the course view, an act’s being legal means that it accords with the rules of a legal system; an act’s being moral means that it is ethically as it ought to be. Those are distinct categories. So if the ordinance really prohibited food distribution without a permit, her act may have been illegal even if morally admirable.

But the city official is equally wrong to infer from illegality to immorality. The lecture explicitly rejects identifying legality and morality, since legal systems can contain evil or unjust laws. If illegality automatically made an act immoral, then morally justified disobedience would be impossible by definition, which the course denies.

The supported position is therefore neither simple identity nor total severance. Law and morality can come apart in particular cases, but the concept of law is still to be understood in moral terms. That means law is not merely whatever rules happen to be enforced; its analysis must leave room for criticism of unjust laws while also explaining why law normally claims authority and guides conduct.

So the best verdict is: Ava’s action can be morally right yet legally prohibited. The official’s argument fails, but Ava’s attempt to redefine “legal” in purely moral terms fails too.
problems.explanation: Tests the lecture’s position that legality and morality are distinct but not unrelated. A strong answer must reject both crude identification and crude separation, applying that middle position to civil disobedience-like facts.
problems.hint: The easiest mistakes are: 'legal = moral' and 'since they differ, they have nothing to do with each other.'
